title: Does Your Neural Network Extrapolate? Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization
claim: Models that fit a window equally well diverge outside it, but a suitable feature map turns extrapolation into interpolation.
layout: 2 panels, left plot with right stacked schematic boxes, top-to-bottom arrow
description: The left panel is a line plot of f(x) against x from -π to 3π. A blue-tinted ID (train) zone and a red-tinted OOD zone are separated by a vertical line at π. The green sin(x) curve overlaps a dashed black Taylor-9 polynomial in the ID zone, with a note reading 'max 1.25% deviation'. In the OOD zone the curves split. Taylor-9 and SINDy shoot upward. MLP and TabPFN flatten out. TimesFM follows the sine when trained on sin. A legend identifies the models. The right panel has two rounded boxes joined by a downward arrow. 'Original Space' shows a blue ID interval and a red OOD interval on a number line, labelled 'must extrapolate'. 'Transformed Space' shows a circle where the ID arc and the dashed OOD arc coincide, labelled 'extrapolation = interpolation'.
caption: Left: $\sin(x)$ (green) and its degree-9 Taylor polynomial (black) can be observationally equivalent on the training window (depending on noise and amount of samples) and diverge on $[\pi, 3\pi]$. Models (MLP, SINDy, TabPFN, TimesFM) trained/evaluated on the Original (raw) space without noise are shown. "raw" corresponds to "None" feature map in the tables (untransformed inputs). "On sin" and "on Taylor-9" identify the source of the training or forecasting-context data. Right: in Fourier coordinates $\varphi(x) = (\sin x, \cos x)$, both (ID, OOD) map to the same circle $\mathbb{S}^1$, turning OOD extrapolation into interpolation.
abstract: Deep neural networks can learn salient features from an in-distribution (ID) training window without identifying the data-generating structure needed for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Understanding this limitation requires examining the identifiability of the data-generating process (DGP). From a single training window, the DGP that yields the correct OOD extrapolation is not identifiable: infinitely many DGPs are observationally equivalent within a fixed tolerance on that window yet diverge arbitrarily beyond it, and no ID criterion alone can reliably distinguish them. A structural commitment---the feature map, label map, and model class $(Ï, Ï, \mathcal{M})$---specifies the assumed DGP and governs OOD generalization while leaving ID performance essentially unchanged. When architecture, pretraining, data augmentation, input formats, or domain knowledge implicitly supply the correct commitment, the model generalizes beyond the training window. When it cannot infer OOD-relevant structure from ID evidence, it fails to generalize. When the commitment is correct {\em and} identifiable, OOD error vanishes. We demonstrate this mechanism in models trained from scratch and in foundation models across four natural-science settings (chemistry, physics, biology, and histopathology), as well as in a positional-encoding study spanning Transformer, Mamba, and S4D architectures. Finally, a controlled study shows that correct features are necessary but not sufficient for OOD generalization.
